data.title: More lawmakers report suspicious packages at offices
data.description:
Several lawmakers said Friday their offices across the country had received suspicious mailings following reports earlier this week of letters containing unknown substances at U.S. election offices.

Sens. Amy Klobuchar (D-Minn.), Mike Rounds (R-S.D.), Pete Ricketts (R-Neb.), Tina Smith (D-Minn.) and over 15 House lawmakers said their district or state offices received these packages. 

Klobuchar said in a Friday social media statement that officials intercepted the letter before it reached her Minnesota office. 

“Thanks to the postal workers and investigators who identified and intercepted it, no one in our office was in immediate danger,” the Democratic senator wrote. “We’re grateful to everyone involved for their quick response and we will continue working closely with law enforcement as the investigation continues.”

Rounds shared an image of a letter sent to his Sioux Falls, N.D., office, and said the regional team contacted local authorities, who investigated and evacuated the office. 

“This situation is deeply concerning and follows a trend of intimidating tactics that impact our team members,” he wrote on social media. “This has no place in our nation. America is better than this.” 

California Reps. Laura Friedman (D), Jimmy Panetta (D), Gil Cisneros (D) and Linda Sánchez (D) all reported receiving suspicious packages at their district offices and said their staff members were safe.  

Panetta, who represents the state’s 19th District, said a staff member at his Santa Cruz office opened an envelope that contained a “suspicious white powder.”

“Upon realizing that there was powder in the envelope, she immediately put the envelope in the garbage can, cleared fellow staff members out of the office, and called 911,” the lawmaker said in a social media post. “My priority is the safety and security of my staff and, thankfully, she and the other staff have been initially cleared by medical officials.”

In Florida, Democratic Reps. Maxwell Frost and Darren Soto shared similar reports from their district offices in Orlando and Kissimmee, respectively. 

Soto shared on social media that his district office received “advance notice” from Frost’s Orlando office to “monitor our mail.”

“We are working with federal, state, and local law enforcement to support an investigation,” Soto continued. “Political violence has no place in our democracy, and we hope those who perpetrated this crime are brought to justice.” 

On Thursday, spokespeople for two Democratic lawmakers, Sens. Chris Murphy (Conn.) and Alex Padilla (Calif.) told The Hill’s broadcast partner, NewsNation, they were notified that authorities intercepted suspicious packages addressed to their offices.  

These suspicious mailings come just weeks ahead of the midterm elections. Before the 2024 presidential election, election officials in several states reported receiving packages that contained white powder.  

Rep. Pramila Jayapal (D-Wash.), whose district office also reported a similar package, decried the timing of these suspicious mailings in a statement shared on social media. 

“This seemingly deliberate and widespread attack on our democracy and elections is unacceptable,” the Washington lawmaker wrote. 

An FBI spokesperson told The Hill on Thursday that the agency was broadly inspecting reports of suspicious packages but declined to comment on specific instances.  

“We are also working with our partners to identify the individual or individuals responsible for the letters,” the spokesperson said Thursday. “This FBI will continue to safeguard the public and secure elections for American citizens.” 

The Hill has reached out to the FBI and U.S. Capitol Police regarding these new reports.

The U.S. Central Command (Centcom) Commander Adm. Brad Cooper said on Friday that the U.S. naval blockade has cost Iran $25 billion in crude oil export revenue.

“As a point of emphasis, with the exception of the humanitarian assistance we’ve allowed in, Iran has no exports and no imports by sea,” Cooper said in a video. “The sum total of these actions has imposed devastating costs on Iran’s security apparatus and the IRGC specifically.”

The U.S. military restarted the blockade in July, which is enforced by Navy ships and other assets in the region, to prevent Iranian ships from entering and departing the country’s ports. 

 

Cooper said the U.S. government has helped freeze $350 million of cryptocurrency owned by Iran, and the U.S. military has helped 400 vessels transit the Strait of Hormuz in the last week. 

 

The admiral said the pressure campaign is paying off, with the Islamic Republic feeling the pain across all economic sectors. 

 

“Iran’s government is withholding salaries, pensions and benefits to workers in industries such as oil and energy, manufacturing, construction, security, and the IRGC itself,” Cooper said in the video.

The Big Story 

FERC moves to ease gas approvals

Federal energy regulators have proposed setting up a program to speed up approvals for expanding the nation’s gas export facilities.

© Jacquelyn Martin, Associated Press

The Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) on Thursday proposed to limit notice and protest periods to either 60 days or 90 days for expansions at liquified natural gas (LNG) export terminals. 

 

FERC Chair Laura Swett (R) said the move would “enable the country to scale up its existing facilities more quickly to supply our allies who are in desperate need.”

 

She added the action would “maintain safety and environmental protections.” 

 

The commission also proposed to no longer require gas projects to submit certain air pollution information as part of the environmental review process. 

 

Specifically, the commission is proposing to omit air dispersion models, which simulate how a project’s emissions may interact with other atmospheric pollution to determine air quality impacts.

data.title: 5 days of Katie Zacharia: The rapid fall of Trump's 'lawyer' press secretary
data.description:
Katie Zacharia won’t be remembered as one of the “all-time greats” in the White House press room, as one of her colleagues predicted this week, but she will go down in the annals of presidential press secretary history.

Her tenure of five days in the role easily beats the previous record held by Anthony Scaramucci, who spent 11 days in President Trump’s communications shop during his first term.

Zacharia kicked off her time at the podium with some big news, announcing the departure of Kimberly Guilfoyle as U.S. ambassador to Greece, but she quickly became the news as questions swirled over her legal career.

Here’s how it all went down:

Day 1

Trump announced on Monday, a federal holiday, that Zacharia would be holding her first press briefing the next day. 

“Katie has been with me, in spirit, from the very beginning, and will do a fantastic job!” he wrote on Truth Social.

Before the appointment, she was the senior communications adviser to Truth Social, after having briefly served as a spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security. 

Zacharia was seen on the South Lawn as Trump departed for a camping rally in Ohio on Monday afternoon but stayed behind at the White House. She received her initial briefing materials that same day. 

Day 2 

Zacharia held her first press briefing before a packed room of journalists. It was a shaky opening, as she haltingly read from a script and accidentally referred to her husband, Tyler Zacharia, as “my president.”

She broke the major news about Guilfoyle, which led the ensuing news cycle, but only spoke for roughly 14 minutes and took questions from three conservative-leaning outlets.

Within minutes, critics were asking if Zacharia was up for the job, but her defenders said the nerves were to be expected during her first outing in the pressure-packed press room.

That afternoon, a reporter asked Trump where his new press secretary, who often touted herself as a lawyer, passed the bar exam. He turned around to Zacharia, standing behind him outside the White House, to answer.

She responded, “when I moved to China.”  

The newsletter Popular Information has previously raised questions about her legal career, reporting that no record was found of her passing a bar exam anywhere. 

The White House said Zacharia moved to China with her husband after graduating from Pepperdine University’s law school.

She had referred to herself as a lawyer on TV previously, and Trump called her an attorney when he announced she would be taking the position.

Her LinkedIn account shows she worked as an associate at the Zhong Lun Law Firm in Beijing from August 2011 to June 2013 and was general counsel of Fix California from 2024-2025.

Both resumé items would become the subject of much chatter in the days ahead. 

Day 3 

The Wall Street Journal reported Wednesday that she sat for the California bar exam after graduating from law school in 2011 but didn’t pass.

The Campaign for Accountability filed a complaint with the State Bar of California on Wednesday asking for an investigation into whether Zacharia’s claims of being a lawyer broke state law.

The complaint notes that if the reporting is accurate — that Zacharia has “repeatedly held herself out to the public as entitled to practice law without a license to do so” — it could be a crime under California law.

The White House pushed back on the complaint, with communications director Steven Cheung calling Campaign for Accountability a “radical leftist-organization run by rabid numbskulls suffering from a severe case of Trump Derangement Syndrome.”

Zacharia’s time in China also came under the spotlight. Legal experts told The Hill that while she may have worked at a law firm in China, that didn’t necessarily make her a lawyer.

Day 4

Zacharia went on defense Thursday, with a pair of interviews on conservative outlets.  

She told Jack Posobiac on Real America’s Voice that she didn’t have time to get fully prepared ahead of the shaky Tuesday briefing.

“I never had a full briefing beforehand, and I went out and I effectuated the briefing,” she said. 

“It was absolutely my goal to keep it short, considering he is his own best spokesperson,” she added of Trump.

She said the initial briefing materials were given to her on Monday evening, but only finalized on Tuesday at 8 a.m., less than two hours before she appeared for the 9:30 a.m. briefing. She said she had been up since 3 a.m. preparing.

She told Posobiac that the results of her bar exam were “somewhat inconsequential” because she knew she’d be moving to China.

“After moving to China, I didn’t really think much of the bar results or consider that something that I needed to focus on,” she said.

“It’s unfortunate that people dub this as some kind of conspiracy or want to put me in a camp,” she said. “The truth is, I was very careful how I executed this, and I never came across as someone who was an attorney-at-law.”

Zacharia faced a surprisingly hostile Sean Hannity on Fox News on Thursday evening.

“You called it a conspiracy theory as it relates to being a lawyer,” Hannity said, referencing the interview Zacharia did with Posobiac, pointing out what he said were 15 social media posts “where you identify yourself as an attorney.” 

“I think they were retweets, and I corrected the record,” she responded.

Day 5

Zacharia appeared on Fox News again Friday morning and was again met with tough questions. 

“Fox & Friends” host Lawrence Jones asked if she should have told the White House about her legal qualifications during the hiring process.

“Those questions weren’t asked,” she said. “I’m being hired as White House press secretary, not White House counsel. The conversations and the reason I was — the reason that I was hired was to represent the president in the press.”

She said the “legacy media wants to put the focus and attention on me because they wanted to be distracted from the major wins that President Trump is making for America.”

If the interviews were meant to win over Trump, it didn’t work. 

Later Friday, Trump told reporters before departing the White House that he told Zacharia to “reconsider” the role.

“I said, ‘Honestly, if I were you, I’d reconsider,’” Trump told reporters Friday, referring to a conversation he said he had with Zacharia earlier. 

“I said, ‘You think about it, but I would reconsider,’” he continued.  

Minutes later came the first reports that she was out of the job.

A White House official said she was “transitioning out” of the role.

Zacharia hasn’t made any public comments, and did not respond to a request for comment from The Hill.

A source familiar told The Hill that Zacharia was to join Vice President Vance and second lady Usha Vance for dinner at their residence Friday evening.

data.title: Energy regulators speed up approvals for gas export facility expansions
data.description:
U.S. energy regulators have proposed establishing a program that would speed up approvals for expanding the nation’s gas export facilities

The Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) proposed Thursday to limit notice and protest periods to either 60 or 90 days for requested expansions to liquified natural gas (LNG) export terminals. 

FERC Chair Laura Swett (R) said the move would “enable the country to scale up its existing facilities more quickly to supply our allies who are in desperate need.”

She added that the action would “maintain safety and environmental protections.” 

The commission also proposed to no longer require planned gas projects to submit certain air pollution information as part of the environmental review process. 

Specifically, the commission is looking to omit air dispersion models, which simulate how a project’s emissions may interact with other atmospheric pollution to determine air quality impacts. 

“These models have proven time and again to be an unnecessary source of confusion, delay, and litigation risk,” Swett said. 

However, fellow FERC commissioner Judy Chang (D) disagreed, saying this type of modeling is “the best tool we have for understanding the likely local and regional air impacts of the projects we permit.”

Both moves by the commission received pushback from environmental advocates.

“It is unconscionable for FERC to further fast-track harmful LNG development and also cut requirements for gas developers to submit modeling to understand the local air quality impacts of methane gas projects,” Claire Dorner, Sierra Club’s associate legislative and advocacy director of its “Beyond Dirty Fuels” campaign, said in a written statement. 

“Eroding these guardrails will make our historically high energy prices even worse, increase harm to local ecosystems and communities, and exacerbate the climate crisis,” Dorner said. 

FERC is made up of presidentially appointed commissioners but is technically independent from the Trump administration. It is comprised of three Republicans and two Democrats.

data.title: Bipartisan senators ask Pentagon to answer for Ukraine Starlink restrictions
data.description:
{beacon}

Technology

Technology

 

The Big Story 

GOP senators press Pentagon over Starlink restrictions in Ukraine 

Four Republican senators joined their Democratic colleagues in pressing the Trump administration for information about whether Pentagon officials ordered restrictions on Ukraine’s access to the satellite-based Starshield network.

© Tom Brenner, Associated Press

Ukraine needs access to fast Starshield data speeds to operate drones, along with fixed-wing and rotary-wing aircraft — which are critical to its national defense.

 

Ukraine’s full access to Starshield-provided data was quickly restored Wednesday, prompting speculation on Capitol Hill that President Trump didn’t make the call to cut off intelligence sharing with Ukraine but that the decision may have come from senior officials.

 

Four Republican senators — including two senior members of the Senate Intelligence Committee — signed a bipartisan letter to Platte Moring, the Pentagon’s inspector general, demanding he investigate whether any Defense Department or other U.S. government officials “directed” or “authorized” changes to intelligence-sharing arrangements or Starlink and Starshield services affecting Ukraine.

 

Starshield is the military version of SpaceX’s Starlink, which provides internet connectivity from low-orbit satellites.

 

Senate Appropriations Committee Chair Susan Collins (R-Maine), a senior member of the Intelligence Committee, signed the letter, along with fellow panel member Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas), as well as Republican Sens. Lisa Murkowski (Alaska) and Thom Tillis (N.C.).

 

The GOP lawmakers expressed “grave concern” over reports that Ukraine lost access to high-speed internet connectivity, which enables it to operate military vehicles flying faster than 63 mph or faster than 100 mph. The loss hampered its ability to fend off Russian strikes.

 

A Senate source familiar with internal discussions about how to respond to Ukraine’s sudden loss of access to critical military intelligence said senators in both parties have questions about whether Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth or other senior Pentagon officials — such as Elbridge Colby, the undersecretary of defense for policy — were involved in the decision.  

 

The Hill’s Alexander Bolton has the full story.

Judge rejects push by CFTC to toss Biden-era settlement with Gemini

© Illustration / Pavlo Gonchar/SOPA Images, LightRocket via Getty Images

A federal judge Thursday rejected a request by the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) to throw out a Biden-era settlement with the cryptocurrency exchange Gemini.

 

The agency asked the court in May to vacate a consent order with the exchange, saying it found officials used “inappropriate tactics” to obtain the settlement.

 

It also argued it would not have brought the complaint under current enforcement policies.

 

U.S. District Judge Alvin Hellerstein was unmoved, finding this was not “sufficient grounds for relief.”

 

“Gemini’s receipt of additional materials after the fact may have caused it to regret that it settled, but it did not create a post-judgement change in factual circumstances,” he wrote.

 

He also said the CFTC’s recent determination that “this action should not have been brought does not require vacatur or other relief.”

 

“The CFTC retains discretion over its enforcement priorities and remains free to account for its current policies in deciding whether to seek enforcement of the Consent Order,” Hellerstein added.

 

The agency initially sued Gemini — which was founded by billionaire investors Tyler and Cameron Winklevoss — in 2022. It accused the exchange of making false or misleading statements about a Bitcoin futures contract.

 

Shortly before trial, the two sides agreed to the consent order, finding the exchange violated the Commodities Exchange Act. Gemini also paid a $5 million penalty.

data.title: Senate Democrats unveil new plans for strengthening Medicare
data.description:
Presented by Coalition to Strengthen Americas Healthcare
{beacon}

Healthcare

Healthcare

The Big Story 

Senate Democrats unveil new plans for strengthening Medicare

Led by Sen. Ron Wyden (R-Ore.), ranking member of the Senate Finance Committee, Senate Democrats on Friday published their aims of revamping the long-term care system in the U.S., encompassing both home care and nursing homes. 

© Natasha Kaiser

In a request for information (RFI), Wyden stated, “It has been decades since Congress enacted a comprehensive, system-level investment in long-term care infrastructure and financing. And a system-level investment is what is needed.” 

 

The document serves as something of a blueprint for what Democrats hope to achieve in the Medicare space if they reclaim Congress in the upcoming midterms. 

 

At the top of their list is the goal of making long-term care universally available to all Americans. 

 

“Throughout 95 listening sessions, Senate Democrats heard repeatedly about the importance of establishing universal coverage for LTC. Democrats’ goal is to make sure that the LTC system serves all people across age and disability, and across diagnoses, functional needs, and life stages,” the RFI read. 

 

According to the Federal Long Term Care Insurance Program, the national average cost of a semi-private room in a nursing home was $112,4201 in 2025. 

 

Wyden’s RFI noted that many families “spend down” to qualify for Medicaid Home and Community-Based Services, essentially spending income that rises above a certain threshold on healthcare costs in order to qualify for these benefits. 

 

“Senate Democrats are determined to deliver an equitable and affordable home care guarantee for all Americans in need, improve the quality of long-term care across the board, and make sure there are workers in good jobs to meet that need,” Wyden said in a statement.  

 

“That starts by hearing from all corners of the country on the ideas put forward in this document. I look forward to creative, robust and thorough responses that put Americans who need long-term care at the center.”

data.title: Watchdog: Zacharia's exit doesn't 'wipe clean' dispute over legal credentials
data.description:
A D.C.-based ethics watchdog group that accused Katie Zacharia of misrepresenting herself as a lawyer is urging the State Bar of California to press ahead with an investigation into her credentials after she was ousted as White House press secretary.  

The Campaign for Accountability, which filed a Bar complaint against Zacharia earlier this week, said her exit from the White House does not resolve allegations that she may have violated California law by portraying herself as a lawyer despite never being licensed to practice law.  

“The White House clearly recognized that keeping Katie Zacharia as Press Secretary was untenable given the facts that have come out about her conduct,” Michelle Kuppersmith, the group’s executive director, said in a Friday statement to The Hill.  

“Even so, her departure does not wipe clean the fact that she consistently, and apparently falsely, held herself out as a lawyer,” Kuppersmith added. “This is a crime in California, so we continue to urge the state’s Bar to investigate and impose any appropriate penalties.”  

The group filed its complaint on Wednesday, the day after Zacharia’s brief tenure got off to a rocky start with a shaky first press briefing and scrutiny into her professional history.  

Zacharia, a graduate of Pepperdine Law School, has often referred to herself in media appearances as a “lawyer” despite never having passed the bar exam. Her LinkedIn profile also referenced her role as “general counsel” for Fix California, a conservative nonprofit founded by Trump ally and former administration official Richard Grenell.  

She has claimed to have worked as an associate on the International Practice Team of Beijing-based Zhong Lun Law Firm, and President Trump described her as an “attorney” when he announced her as former Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt’s replacement.

When asked by reporters on the South Lawn this week which state she took the bar exam in, Zacharia replied, “When I moved to China.” She later said she misheard the question due to the noise of Marine One and assumed it was about where she went after law school.  

In subsequent interviews, she admitted she never passed the California bar exam, telling The New York Times the results were “somewhat inconsequential” since she was planning to move overseas at the time.

“It was never my intent to go into the practice of law,” Zacharia told Fox News’ Sean Hannity Thursday night. “When I went to go engage in media and give legal analysis, I consulted attorneys and legal professionals as to whether or not they agreed that I could be labeled a lawyer, both because I had a valid Juris Doctor from a good law school, a reputable law school, Pepperdine Law School, and in conjunction with the fact that I did have actual substantive legal experience.” 

The watchdog group alleges her use of the terms may have been unlawful because each representation “conveys to an ordinary listener that Ms. Zacharia is a licensed attorney entitled to practice law.” 

It is commonly believed the term “lawyer” refers to someone who has graduated from law school, while an “attorney” is someone who has passed the bar exam and is licensed to practice law in a specific jurisdiction. 

But the American Bar Association (ABA) makes no such distinction, using the titles interchangeably to describe any “licensed professional who advises and represents others in legal matters.” Many state licensing statutes, including California’s, don’t either.  

California law asserts that “no person shall practice law” in the state unless that person is “an active member of the State Bar” and makes it a misdemeanor offense to unlawfully portray oneself as “practicing or entitled to practice law.” 

It remains to be seen what outcome could come from the complaint, if the State Bar of California even chooses to pursue it at all. Data compiled by Vitreo, an independent hub for judicial data, shows that disciplinary agencies process tens of thousands of complaints each year, and the vast majority are dismissed, screened out or resolved privately.

Because Zacharia is not a member of the California Bar, the agency can’t take any professional disciplinary action against her even if it identifies wrongdoing. It could, however, refer her for prosecution on criminal charges.  

The White House confirmed Friday afternoon that Zacharia was “transitioning out” of the role just five days after President Trump announced her as his pick to fill the press secretary role.

data.title: Oil reaches $110 per barrel
data.description:
Welcome to The Hill’s Business & Economy newsletter
{beacon}

Business & Economy

Business & Economy

 

The Big Story 

Oil hits $110 per barrel for first time since May

An international oil benchmark hit $110 per barrel on Friday, as the industry faces persistent shocks from the U.S.-Iran and Russia-Ukraine wars. 

© Kamran Jebreili, Associated Press file

The price of Brent crude oil, the international standard, hit $110 on the nose during Friday trading. That marked the first time it has reached that level since May 20, less than three months after the U.S. and Israel launched the Iran conflict. 

 

The commodity is trading at roughly $109.75 as of late Friday afternoon. 

 

Brent crude prices peaked in late April, when the benchmark topped $120 per barrel.  

 

Oil prices shot up during the early months of the conflict with Iran and sunk down below $80 per barrel throughout much of June and July — as the U.S. and Iran were operating under a ceasefire both sides accused the other of violating.  

 

But as the war, now approaching the eight-month mark, has persisted, oil prices have surpassed $100 yet again.  

 

West Texas Intermediate crude, the North American benchmark, also topped $100 per barrel on Friday for the first time since Sep. 21. 

 

The increase in oil prices has translated to higher prices at the pump for Americans. Regular gas in the U.S. costs about $4.33 per gallon on average, AAA reported Friday.  

 

Diesel also costs more than $6.30 on average, nearly $2.70 higher than a year ago, according to AAA.

data.title: Press secretary under Clinton says Zacharia was 'set up to fail'
data.description:
Katie Zacharia was set up to fail by the Whtie House and President Trump, who made her White House press secretary without preparing her, former Clinton-era White House Press Secretary Joe Lockhart said Friday.

“I don’t mean this to sound partisan or overly critical of the president, but she is, in fact a victim here,” Lockhart said during an appearance on CNN. “She was thrown out there in a place where she wasn’t prepared.”

Lockhart said when he got the job of press secretary, he took two months off to go to school, sit down with the national security team, budget team and essentially get prepared.

“I wasn’t going to go out, the president wasn’t going to let me go out, the staff wasn’t — until I was absolutely ready, and that’s when I went out,” he said. “She did this in a couple of hours. “

“She was set up to fail, and she has failed. But it shouldn’t be surprising,” he added. “There ought to be a little bit of sympathy here for her that she was not given the ability to succeed here.

Zacharia, who was appointed to the position a week ago, is “transitioning out” of her role after President Trump told reporters that he told her to “reconsider” the position, a White House official told The Hill.

She got off to a rocky start after facing scrutiny about her claims of being a lawyer as reports surfaced about her not being licensed to practice law in any U.S. state. A watchdog group called the Campaign for Accountability filed a complaint with the State Bar of California asking for an investigation into her claim.

The Wall Street Journal reported that Zacharia failed her California bar exam after she received her law degree from Pepperdine University. She said Thursday that the results of the test are “somewhat inconsequential.”

Zacharia ran her first press briefing on Tuesday which ran for 14 minutes where she took three questions from reporters and dropped the news about the resignation of U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle.

Zacharia lasted just five days in the role.
